claim: Long-context serving is moving from short conversations toward applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, long-document question answering and agent reasoning.
quote: Large language model (LLM) serving is gradually shifting from short conversations to long-context applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020), long-document question answering (Bai et al., 2024), and agent reasoning (Yao et al., 2023).

claim: In these settings prefill must process the entire context, and its computational cost grows rapidly with input length.
quote: Prefill must process the entire context, and its computational cost grows rapidly with input length.

claim: A study of serving cost reports that prefill takes tens of percent of GPU time in production workloads, and more in agentic ones dominated by long, repeated tool and document context.
quote: Prefill, the encoding of the prompt before the first output token, accounts for a substantial share of the cost of serving language models: tens of percent of GPU time in reported production workloads, and more in agentic ones dominated by long, repeated tool and document context (DeepSeek-AI, 2025;Ayoub et al., 2025).

claim: A transformer's KV representation of a token is a function of its entire prefix, so exact reuse is confined to contexts that share a prefix verbatim.
quote: a transformer's KV representation of a token is a function of its entire prefix, so exact reuse is confined to contexts that share a prefix verbatim.

claim: The agent harness must then manage context, since session history accumulates while each model call sees only a bounded window.
quote: As trajectories grow, a central challenge for the agent harness is context management: session history accumulates continuously, while each model invocation operates over a bounded context window.

claim: Recursive Language Models treat long prompts as part of an external environment and let the LLM programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: The RLM authors report that it has comparable cost across four long-context tasks.
quote: across four diverse long-context tasks while having comparable cost

claim: Context Language Models (CLMs) are language models that natively manage their own context, implemented by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to it.
quote: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context. We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The CLM authors also co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for serving, reporting a 35% reduction in server-side compute relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.
quote: Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: The CLM evaluation compares against MEM1, Self-Compact, ACM, and recursive language models (RLM) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: The original RLM paper proposes Recursive Language Models as a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and lets the LLM programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.
quote: We propose Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general inference paradigm that treats long prompts as part of an external environment and allows the LLM to programmatically examine, decompose, and recursively call itself over snippets of the prompt.

claim: A reproduction study extends the framework by varying recursion depth, which the original paper left as future work.
quote: While the original paper relies on a default recursion depth of 1 and suggests deeper recursion as a future direction, this study specifically investigates the impact of scaling the recursion depth.

claim: The reproduction reports that depth-1 RLMs help on complex reasoning, while deeper recursion or use on simple retrieval degrades performance and inflates time and tokens.
quote: While depth-1 RLMs effectively boost accuracy on complex reasoning tasks, applying deeper recursion (depth=2) or using RLMs on simple retrieval tasks paradoxically degrades performance and exponentially inflates execution time (e.g., from 3.6s to 344.5s) and token costs.

claim: A separate systems extension, RLM-Extended, states that existing reference implementations of RLM have practical limitations in termination, reproducibility, and deployment.
quote: existing reference implementations have practical limitations in termination, reproducibility, and deployment.

claim: Context Language Models are implemented by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.
quote: We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The CLM study compares CLMs against baselines including recursive language models (RLM) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: The CLM paper introduces Context Language Models as models that natively manage their own context.
quote: We introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), language models that natively manage their own context.

claim: Context Language Models implement their approach by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.
quote: We implement this by treating the context as a file and allowing the model to make unrestricted updates to this file.

claim: The CLM paper compares CLMs against MEM1, Self-Compact, ACM, and recursive language models (RLM) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone.
quote: We compare CLMs against MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026), Self-Compact (Li et al., 2026b), ACM (Li et al., 2026c), and recursive language models (RLM) (Zhang et al., 2025a) with a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone (Merrill et al., 2026).
locator: sec. Coding and Deep Research Tasks, para 23

claim: On cost, the CLM authors report matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on TerminalBench 2.1 with fewer FLOPs.
quote: while matching the strongest baseline's accuracy on the terminal-coding benchmark TerminalBench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) with 29.5% fewer FLOPs.

claim: On EdgeBench-10 with Qwen3.6-27B, the paper reports that CLM reached a higher score than summarization at far lower prefix-reuse compute.
quote: With Qwen3.6-27B, CLM reaches 44.6 using 179 prefix-reuse PFLOPs per trial, versus 42.3 and 437 PFLOPs for summarization; the subagent variant reaches 44.2 at 181 PFLOPs.

claim: Suffix Cache Reuse is the serving co-design that reuses cached states of surviving tokens after an edit.
quote: As shown in Figure 4, when 𝐵 is replaced by 𝐵 ′ after an edit, SCR reuses the cached states of all surviving tokens, including 𝐶 , and only reprefills the newly inserted or appended tokens 𝐵 ′ .
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The authors note that the surviving suffix tokens keep stale cache states encoding the previous prefix.
quote: Surviving suffix tokens 𝐶 thus retain stale cache states that encode the previous prefix, which can even be beneficial in some cases, as it retains richer information from the past.
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The reported serving gain is a 35% reduction in server-side compute relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.
quote: Finally, we co-design Suffix Cache Reuse for CLM serving, further reducing server-side compute by 35% relative to standard SGLang at matched performance.

claim: The CLM paper reports prefix-reuse FLOPs under standard serving throughout, with additional SCR savings reported separately.
quote: Throughout the paper, we report prefix-reuse FLOPs under standard serving; additional SCR savings are reported separately in Section 5.3.
locator: sec. (More) Efficient CLM Serving with Suffix Cache Reuse, para 21

claim: The Leyline authors state that agentic conversations evolve through policy-driven editing, with failed tool calls retried and stale outputs dropped.
quote: Agentic LLMs break this assumption. Their conversations evolve through policy-driven editing: failed tool calls are retried, stale outputs dropped, trajectories pivoted.

claim: Leyline reports that production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit.
quote: Production agentic harnesses fall back to re-prefill on every edit, paying full prefix-recomputation cost; kernel-level eviction methods make their own decisions and cannot accept policy directives from outside the kernel.

claim: The EPIC authors report up to 8x TTFT improvement and 7x throughput gain over existing systems, with negligible or no accuracy loss.
quote: Experiments show that EPIC achieves up to 8x improvements in Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and 7x throughput gains over existing systems, with negligible or no accuracy loss.

claim: The CacheTune authors warn that directly reusing KV cache in non-prefix settings causes significant degradation in generation quality.
quote: KV Cache reuse offers a direct path to reduce redundant prefill, yet traditional prefix caching applies only to strict-prefix scenarios; directly reusing KV Cache in non-prefix settings breaks the cross-chunk global attention relationships and causes significant degradation in generation quality.

claim: The SemPIC authors state that, under a standard causal decoder, naively stitched caches are position aligned but contextually incomplete, and their quality can collapse.
quote: under a standard causal decoder, naively stitched caches are position aligned but contextually incomplete, and their quality can collapse.

claim: The Leyline authors report that their splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by 11.2 points and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.
quote: The splice kernel lifts replay cache-hit by +11.2 pp and cuts latency by up to 241 ms.

claim: The SMem authors report that deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5x at 512 blocks, while describing the setting as probing the cost model rather than a served regime.
quote: deletion beats suffix recomputation by 8.5$\times$ at 512 blocks and 452$\times$ at 4096 blocks (32-256$\times$ the trained length, probing the cost model rather than a served regime).

claim: The CAT authors report that SWE-Compressor reaches a 57.6% solved rate on SWE-Bench-Verified under a 32B agent post-training setting.
quote: On the challenging SWE-Bench-Verified benchmark, SWE-Compressor achieves a 57.6% solved rate, reaching state-of-the-art performance under the setting of agent post-training on a 32B model.

claim: The CAT authors also report that under a 150-step interaction budget, CAT maintains competitive performance and uses the fewest tokens of all methods.
quote: Under a smaller interaction budget (150 steps), CAT both maintains competitive performance and uses the fewest tokens across all methods.
locator: sec. Context Comparison between CAT and ReAct., para 46

claim: The ACM authors state that their analysis shows effective context management reduces peak token pressure and yields more consistent solutions across independent trials.
quote: Further analysis reveals that effective context management reduces peak token pressure, enables extended explorations, and yields more consistent solutions across independent trials.

claim: The Context Language Models paper describes reinforcement learning in which, because context edits change the input across turns, stepwise GRPO is used.
quote: Since context edits change the input across turns, we use stepwise GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).
locator: sec. In-Context Learning and Reinforcement Learning for CLMs, para 17
